content:
By Daniel Cerqueira Afonso

Rome, November 24, 2026: “Recognized” is a convenient word, but it misleads when it suggests a unique seal. Each appearance on the list was judged differently, and some never received a decree.

For the history, decrees, and criteria in detail, see the main page on the subject.

Until 2024, judgment first and foremost rested with the local bishop. This was as stipulated by the Norms of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, approved by Paul VI on February 24, 1978, and dated February 25, sent to the bishops in a reserved form and officially published only in 2011 (CONGREGAȚIO PRO DOCTRINA FIDEI, 1978, III.1, CONGREGATIO PRO DOCTRINA FIDEI, 2012, p. 497, and DICASTÉRIO PARA A DOUTRINA DA FÉ, 2024, Introduction).

Since May 19, 2024, the Norms of the Dicastery for Doctrine, dated May 17, entirely replace those of 1978 (Doctrine of the Faith Dicastery, 2024, Article 27). The diocesan bishop examines the case and formulates the final judgment, which the Dicastery must approve (art. 1).

Normally, the bishop’s judgment follows one of six formulas (n. 16 and art. 18).

Nothing stands in the way:

• without certain knowledge of supernatural origin, but with signs of the Holy Spirit’s action (n. 17)

• “Let it be before the eyes”: positive signs, but also confusion or risks (n. 18)

• Healing: significant critical elements, but the phenomenon is already widespread and bears fruit, and therefore prohibition is discouraged, although the bishop should not encourage it (n. 19)

• Under mandate: the problem lies in a person or group that makes improper use of the phenomenon (n. 20)

• “It is forbidden and obstructed”: the risks are grave and adherence is not permitted (n. 21)

• Declaration on the non-supernatural nature: It declares the phenomenon to be non-supernatural, based on proven facts (n. 22)

As a rule, neither the bishop, nor the episcopal conferences, nor the Dicastery declare that a phenomenon is of supernatural origin (n. 23). And, even with nihil obstat, the faithful are not obliged to give it assent of faith (n. 12). It is a private revelation.

# The List

This is a selection of the best-known ones, and the complete table is on the main page. All cases are prior to 2024. Two of them, Guadalupe and Rue du Bac, never had a decree. The others received from the local bishop judgments with proper formulas.

• Our Lady of Guadalupe (Mexico, 1531), was revealed to Saint Juan Diego, canonized on July 30, 2002. There was no decree. There was indirect approval by the Archbishop of Mexico, Alonso de Montúfar, in 1555, and a specific brief granted by Benedict XIV in 1754 (LAURENTIN and SBALCHIERO, 2007, pp. 402-406)

• Rue du Bac, Paris, Our Lady of the Miraculous Medal (France, 1830), Saint Catherine Laboure. Although the apparitions were never officially recognized by decree, the Church’s liturgy does make official mention of the events (LAURENTIN and SBALCHIERO, 2007, p. 540)

• La Salette (France, 1846), to Mélanie and Maximin on September 19, 1846. The Bishop of Grenoble, Mons. de Bruillard, recognized the apparition by decree of September 19, 1851, using the formula “The faithful are justified in believing as indubitable and certain” (DIOCESAN CONGREGATION FOR DOCTRINE OF THE FAITH, 2024, Introduction, and LAURENTIN and SBALCHIERO, 2007, pp. 96 and 507-508)

• Lourdes (France, 1858), to Saint Bernadette. In the mandate of January 18, 1862, the Bishop of Tarbes, Monsignor Laurence, judged that the Immaculate Mother of God had truly appeared to Bernadette (LAURENTIN and SBALCHIERO, 2007, p. 564)

• Pontmain (France, 1871), on January 17, 1871. Judgment of the Bishop of Laval on February 2, 1872 (pp. 746-749)

• Fatima (Portugal, 1917), to the three shepherd children. The Bishop of Leiria declared the children’s visions “credible” on October 13, 1930 (FATIMA SANCTUARY, 2013, pp. 550-551)

• Beauraing (Belgium, from November 29, 1932 to January 3, 1933). Devotion approved in 1943 and apparitions recognized by Mons. Charue, Bishop of Namur, on July 2, 1949 (LAURENTIN and SBALCHIERO, 2007, pp. 120-122)

• Banneux (Belgium, from January 15 to March 2, 1933). Cultus authorized in 1942, recognized on August 22, 1949, both by Mons. Kerkhofs, Bishop of Liège (pp. 111-114)

• Our Lady of Akita (Japan, 1973), to Sister Agnès Sasagawa, from June 12, 1973. On April 22, 1984, Bishop Itô of Niigata declared the facts undeniable and authorized the veneration of Our Lady of Akita. There was no Roman decree (pp. 1022-1025)

• Kibeho (Rwanda, 1981), Alphonsine Mumureke, Nathalie Mukamazimpaka, and Marie Claire Mukangango, beginning on November 28, 1981. On June 29, 2001, Bishop Misago of Gikongoro declared that the Virgin Mary appeared in Kibeho on that day and in the months that followed, and he only recognized these three initial visionaries as authentic. The last public appearance, of Alphonsine, was on November 28, 1989 (MISAGO, 2020, pp. 59 and 62).

Our Lady of Aparecida does not appear on the list because it is not an apparition. The Dictionary describes it as an unexplained discovery, yet it includes it, without comment, in its list of recognized apparitions (LAURENTIN and SBALCHIERO, 2007, pp. 94 and 96).

Frequently Asked Questions

Does recognizing an apparition necessitate believing in it?

No. Even when there is a nihil obstat, the faithful are not obliged to give assent of faith to the phenomenon (DOCTRINAL DICASTERY, 2024, n. 12). See public and private revelation.

Who recognizes an apparition today?

The diocesan bishop examines and proposes the judgment, the Dicastery for Doctrinal Faith approves it, and the bishop publishes it in accordance with the response received (DICASTÉRIO PARA A DOUTRINA DA FÉ, 2024, arts. 1 and 18-21).

Has the Church already examined all the apparitions?

No. The Norms of 2024 note that, since 1950, only six cases have been officially resolved (Dicastery for Doctrinal Faith, 2024, Introduction).
